\chapter{One Stem, Two Tenses}
\label{ch:spanish-future-conditional-stems}
\hlchaptermodality{49}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can use the irregular stems that serve the future and the conditional alike.}

hare, tendre, podre - stems shared by both tenses, so learning one buys the other.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[haré · tendré · podré]{haré · tendré · podré — three stems, two ending sets}

\label{lesson:ES-C17-irregulares}



\begin{quote}
Regular verbs keep the whole infinitive. Three common verbs you already know use a shorter or reshaped stem. Learn only these three today. In each row, the \textbf{same} stem serves the future and the conditional.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: hacer becomes har-}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{future} & \textbf{conditional} \\
\midrule
yo & \textbf{haré} & \textbf{haría} \\
tú & \textbf{harás} & \textbf{harías} \\
él / ella / usted & \textbf{hará} & \textbf{haría} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Use the known noun in \textbf{Haré café} — “I will make coffee” — and \textbf{Haría café} — “I would make coffee.”
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: tener becomes tendr-}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{future} & \textbf{conditional} \\
\midrule
yo & \textbf{tendré} & \textbf{tendría} \\
tú & \textbf{tendrás} & \textbf{tendrías} \\
él / ella / usted & \textbf{tendrá} & \textbf{tendría} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The \textbf{d} in \textbf{tendr-} arose during the history of the compact future and conditional. Treat \textbf{tendr-} as the learned stem, not as permission to insert \textbf{d} into a new verb.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: poder becomes podr-}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{future} & \textbf{conditional} \\
\midrule
yo & \textbf{podré} & \textbf{podría} \\
tú & \textbf{podrás} & \textbf{podrías} \\
él / ella / usted & \textbf{podrá} & \textbf{podría} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Podré hablar español} says “I will be able to speak Spanish.” \textbf{Podría hablar español} says “I could / would be able to speak Spanish.”

These stems reflect inherited reductions and sound changes. The useful modern fact is bounded: \textbf{har- · tendr- · podr-}, each followed by the same endings you already learned.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “haré, haría”
  \item “tendré, tendría”
  \item “podré, podría”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the three learned stems. (\textbf{Har-, tendr-, podr-.}) Does each verb need separate future and conditional stems? (No; one stem serves both.) Do the endings change? (No.) Next: retrieve the complete twelve-atom chapter.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — one infinitive frame, two futures of thought}

\label{lesson:ES-C17-practice}



\begin{quote}
This checkpoint adds no vocabulary and no plural persons. Retrieve the six regular singular rows, then the three learned irregular stems. Use the future for “will” and the conditional for the bounded core meaning “would.”
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the regular frame}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{hablar} & \textbf{comer} & \textbf{vivir} \\
\midrule
yo future & hablaré & comeré & viviré \\
tú future & hablarás & comerás & vivirás \\
él / ella / usted future & hablará & comerá & vivirá \\
yo conditional & hablaría & comería & viviría \\
tú conditional & hablarías & comerías & vivirías \\
él / ella / usted conditional & hablaría & comería & viviría \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

All three regular infinitives remain whole. Future endings are \textbf{-é, -ás, -á}; conditional endings are \textbf{-ía, -ías, -ía}. Plural persons wait.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three learned stems}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{verb} & \textbf{learned stem} & \textbf{future yo} & \textbf{conditional yo} \\
\midrule
hacer & har- & haré & haría \\
tener & tendr- & tendré & tendría \\
poder & podr- & podré & podría \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The stems change; the ending sets do not. Other irregular stems remain outside this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Romance future and conditional forms grew from constructions pairing an infinitive with forms of Latin \textbf{habēre}. Present material contributed to the future; past or imperfect material contributed to the conditional. Many paths and competing forms existed during the change, so this is a bridge for memory, not a one-step story or a recipe using modern \textbf{haber}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “hablaré, comeré, viviré”
  \item “hablaría, comería, viviría”
  \item “haré/haría · tendré/tendría · podré/podría”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the three regular future yo forms. (\emph{Hablaré, comeré, viviré.}) Give the three regular conditional yo forms. (\emph{Hablaría, comería, viviría.}) Which three learned stems replace a whole infinitive? (\textbf{Har-, tendr-, podr-.}) What is the careful historical bridge? (Infinitive plus forms of Latin \textbf{habēre}, reshaped through Romance.) The next chapter can now begin without borrowing plural persons, new auxiliaries, or clock-time vocabulary.
\end{tcolorbox}
